incorporated_articles.title: Guidelines for secure AI system development

units.text: Security must be a core requirement, not just in the development phase, but throughout the life cycle of the system.
units.text_start: Security must be a core requirement
units.text_end: throughout the life cycle of the system

units.text: As well as existing cyber security threats, AI systems are subject to new types of vulnerabilities. The term ‘adversarial machine learning’ (AML), is used to describe the exploitation of fundamental vulnerabilities in ML components, including hardware, software, workflows and supply chains.
units.text_start: AI systems are subject to new types of vulnerabilities
units.text_end: hardware, software, workflows and supply chains

units.section: Who is responsible for developing secure AI?
units.text: As such, in line with ‘secure by design’ principles, providers of AI components should take responsibility for the security outcomes of users further down the supply chain.
units.text_start: providers of AI components should take responsibility
units.text_end: users further down the supply chain

units.section: Model the threats to your system
units.text: As part of your risk management process, you apply a holistic process to assess the threats to your system, which includes understanding the potential impacts to the system, users, organisations, and wider society if an AI component is compromised or behaves unexpectedly. This process involves assessing the impact of AI-specific threats and documenting your decision making.
units.text_start: you apply a holistic process to assess the threats to your system

units.section: Design your system for security as well as functionality and performance
units.text: you implement scanning and isolation/sandboxing when importing third-party models or serialised weights, which should be treated as untrusted third-party code and could enable remote code execution
units.text_start: scanning and isolation/sandboxing when importing third-party models

units.section: Design your system for security as well as functionality and performance
units.text: if using an external API, you apply appropriate controls to data that can be sent to services outside of your organisation’s control, such as requiring users to log in and confirm before sending potentially sensitive information
units.text_start: apply appropriate controls to data that can be sent to services outside

units.text: You assess and monitor the security of your AI supply chains across a system’s life cycle, and require suppliers to adhere to the same standards your own organisation applies to other software.
units.text_start: assess and monitor the security of your AI supply chains
units.text_end: same standards your own organisation applies to other software

units.section: Identify, track and protect your assets
units.text: You understand the value to your organisation of your AI-related assets, including models, data (including user feedback), prompts, software, documentation, logs and assessments (including information about potentially unsafe capabilities and failure modes), recognising where they represent significant investment and where access to them enables an attacker. You treat logs as sensitive data and implement controls to protect their confidentiality, integrity and availability.
units.text_start: You treat logs as sensitive data

units.section: Document your data, models and prompts
units.text: You document the creation, operation, and life cycle management of any models, datasets and meta - or system - prompts. Your documentation includes security-relevant information such as the sources of training data (including fine-tuning data and human or other operational feedback), intended scope and limitations, guardrails, cryptographic hashes or signatures, retention time, suggested review frequency and potential failure modes. Useful structures to help do this include model cards, data cards and software bills of materials (SBOMs).
units.text_start: Useful structures to help do this include model cards, data cards

units.text: Attackers may be able to reconstruct the functionality of a model or the data it was trained on, by accessing a model directly (by acquiring model weights) or indirectly (by querying the model via an application or service).
units.text_start: Attackers may be able to reconstruct the functionality of a model
units.text_end: querying the model via an application or service

units.text: You release models, applications or systems only after subjecting them to appropriate and effective security evaluation such as benchmarking and red teaming (as well as other tests that are out of scope for these guidelines, such as safety or fairness), and you are clear to your users about known limitations or potential failure modes.
units.text_start: only after subjecting them to appropriate and effective security evaluation
units.text_end: known limitations or potential failure modes

units.section: Make it easy for users to do the right things
units.text: Ideally, the most secure setting will be integrated into the system as the only option. When configuration is necessary, the default option should be broadly secure against common threats (that is, secure by default).
units.text_start: the default option should be broadly secure against common threats

units.text: In line with privacy and data protection requirements, you monitor and log inputs to your system (such as inference requests, queries or prompts) to enable compliance obligations, audit, investigation and remediation in the case of compromise or misuse.
units.text_start: you monitor and log inputs to your system
